body:
The account does its main work well: it separates four facts, attaches conjectures to them, and marks several of its own uncertainties. My objections are at the joints where its design provisions fail to carry its own principles, plus one inference that cannot support the weight put on it.

1. The binding principle creates a veto the account never notices. 'Agreements negotiated by two people will not bind a third who was not there' is stated as a law, and the repair path is built on it: re-include before deciding. But chores recur daily. If the friend does not respond to the low-cost draft — likely, since avoiding the topic is exactly what they are doing — the group faces two options, both forbidden: decide without them, violating the principle, or wait, which by the account's own analysis of stale divisions drifts into resentment. The account sets no default division, no non-response rule, and no limit on waiting. Stated as a flat law, the principle converts avoidance into structural blocking power. It is also too strong as fact: people do accept arrangements made without them, particularly when the alternative is doing the negotiating they avoided. The operative variable is perceived legitimacy, not presence — which the account's own fairness-metric section implies.

2. The maintenance mechanism contradicts the diagnosis. The system's upkeep is a recurring review conversation, and the presenting facts include one member avoiding exactly that. The asynchronous draft is deployed only as a re-entry precursor; the account never says why the cheaper channel should not be the routine one, with meetings as escalation rather than default. And if the avoider skips the first review, the account gives no rule for what happens next.

3. The re-entry script embodies the problem it is meant to fix. Among the account's candidate causes is that the friend 'may feel outnumbered by the other two.' Its concrete script then has — realistically — the two engaged flatmates producing a draft split for the third to mark. To someone whose grievance is bloc-formation, a take-it-or-mark-it document authored by the bloc reads as consolidation, whatever its content. The account cautions tone but never treats who designs the system as a variable, and all four proposals are addressed to the asker as designer. A sequencing fix is available: the avoider picks first, or chooses the format, or names one change before any draft exists.

4. Naming a fairness standard is not the same as clarifying agreements, and it may be the riskier move. The meaning-disputes call for local specification — bins, Sunday, one person — and the record does that. But a named global metric (task-count versus time-cost versus unpleasantness) can convert diffuse arguments about specific tasks into a direct conflict about values, with a permanent loser. Ambiguity does real work in functioning households; rotation or preference-swaps can deliver the account's own fairness goals without ever naming a doctrine. The account treats explicitness as uniformly cheap.

5. The record's main failure mode is managed by admonition where design is available. The account correctly predicts that a record used to win arguments deepens avoidance — then assigns control to 'your own use.' The record is shared; the other two's use is not governed by the asker's conduct. A forward-only design (current assignments only; no completion or miss history; entries expiring at review) prevents the prosecution use structurally. Against a risk the account itself names, it chose the weaker safeguard.

6. The final pivot cannot arbitrate. 'If the arguments continue at the same intensity, then the chores were probably never the substance' — no baseline, no window, no check on implementation quality. Argument frequency fluctuates; within any short span, the same data is compatible with 'working, slowly' and 'failed.' Earlier tests in the account are sharper; the pivotal one — the one that would redirect the asker toward questioning the living arrangement — is the least specified.

Two smaller points: the direct question to the avoider dichotomizes ('the chores, or how the conversations have been going') when it could be both or neither — workload, money, feeling undervalued outside chores entirely; and writing-as-low-cost is an assumption about this person's medium preferences (for some, written chore documents read as more formal and accusatory than talk), which the account hedges only at the outcome level, not at first contact.

Where the account already concedes — strategic disputes, the written-too test, the unknown cause of avoidance — these points sharpen rather than correct. And there is a symmetry worth naming: the account criticizes agreements that leave their meaning on unstated cases unspecified, and its own system leaves the silence case unspecified — what happens when the draft gets no reply is exactly as underdetermined as 'I'll handle the bins.' My objections are themselves fallible: if the friend engages with the draft script as designed, points 2 and 3 lose force; if the group's fairness ideals turn out compatible, point 4 is moot; and point 1 could be answered if the objection window was intended as a non-response rule — but the account never says so.
commitments:
Taking up this objection involves the following, with their tests and risks.

Adopting a non-response rule — the current division persists by default, and proposed changes take effect after a stated objection window even without reply — commits me to reading the account's binding principle as a legitimacy concern rather than a law. That fix carries a risk of its own: implementing over silence may read as precisely the bloc behavior point 3 worries about, so I would hold the window long and frame the default as fallback, not pressure. Test: whether the avoider treats a rule that waits for them as safer than open-ended invitation, or whether they respond better to firm defaults — in which case my reading errs in the opposite direction.

Sequencing the avoider's authorship — first pick, format choice, or one named change before any draft — commits me to the claim that who writes the system matters more than the efficiency of the asker writing it. Test: engagement with a document they shaped versus one they were sent. If they decline even first pick, the fix collapses back into the account's original approach.

The forward-only record commits me to trading enforcement capacity for safety: no history means the group also loses the ability to check whether the split is actually being followed, and if under-performance rather than misreading is the real driver, that trade protects the wrong thing. Test: whether disputes shift from past performance ('you missed Tuesday') to future assignments.

Deferring the global fairness metric in favor of rotation or swaps commits me to constructive ambiguity — the claim that a latent conflict is better left latent. I own the cost: if the three hold genuinely incompatible fairness ideals, this delays rather than dissolves the conflict, and rotation has its own friction, including efficiency losses and people losing tasks they like or do well.

Demanding a measurement protocol before using the final pivot — a counted baseline, a fixed window of two or three review cycles, a criterion agreed in advance — commits me to deferring a conclusion that may in fact be correct; if the chores really are a proxy, the delay has its own cost.

Dependencies and concessions: none of these fixes is unilateral; the non-response rule in particular requires the group's acceptance, and the whole objection set is conditional on the avoider's participation mattering as much as the account assumes. Where the account already hedges — the written-avoidance test, the strategic-dispute caveat, the unknown cause of avoidance — I am sharpening, not overturning. If the draft-split script simply works, the surviving criticisms are the missing absence rule and the unmeasured final pivot, and those two are the claims I would defend first.
